strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: measuring degrees of informational contribution in human–AI writing. Its explicit distinction between informational contribution and creativity or legal authorship is appropriate.

The experiments cover four domains, six generation models, two scoring models, repeated generations, and WildChat interactions. Consistent ordering across generation conditions provides useful evidence that the proposed score captures broad differences in prompt–output dependence.

The human evaluation provides encouraging evidence on the evaluated subset: 1,500 pairs receive three annotations each, with 91.47% unanimous agreement and 95.93% agreement between majority judgments and the input-aware score. The appendices document source datasets, generation prompts, model versions, and threshold calibration.
weaknesses: The interpretation of the central score needs stronger justification. Equation (5) computes a pointwise log-likelihood ratio, rather than Shannon mutual information averaged over a joint distribution. It can be negative even with the original generation model, and the unprompted distribution is not established as the marginal of the prompted generation process. Predictive likelihood gain is a plausible heuristic, but these equations do not establish a calibrated percentage of information attributable to a human.

The text-only extension does not establish its claimed minimum. Appendix B derives a lower bound conditional on the chosen plausibility threshold, but Equation (10) equates that bound with the minimum without demonstrating attainability or tightness. Appendix A.5 sets the conditional-surprisal threshold to an empirical mean plus one standard deviation; this is not a general upper bound on plausible generations. Coverage, sensitivity, and comparisons against known-input contribution values are needed.

The text-only score is a transformation of ordinary perplexity. Writing h = -log p(y)/N and c = -log τ, Equation (10) becomes 1 - c/h. For a fixed scoring model and threshold, it therefore produces exactly the same rankings and ROC–AUC as perplexity. The detection results in Table 2 support a familiar likelihood signal, but do not independently validate the interpretation as minimum human contribution.

The human evaluation is selected using the method being evaluated: pairs are included only when the proposed score differs by more than 0.1. The reported agreement consequently does not establish performance on an independently sampled population, particularly close comparisons. Reusing these pairs for the text-only estimator retains this limitation. Evaluation should include independently sampled and within-condition pairs, with comparisons against input/output length ratios, lexical overlap, and likelihood baselines to distinguish contribution measurement from simpler correlates.

Several robustness conclusions exceed the tests performed. Appendix C.3 uses two fixed instruction suffixes rather than attacks adapted through feedback from the score. The surrogate-model experiments primarily establish broad category ordering, without measuring agreement or calibration of individual contribution estimates across scorers. These results support narrower robustness claims.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful experimental appendix. The manuscript does not specify the exact likelihood-scoring templates, treatment of special tokens, or whether probabilities incorporate sampling temperature, and it provides no code or constructed-data release link. These choices directly affect the metric. Correcting the interpretation, strengthening independent validation, and documenting scoring precisely appear feasible next cycle; the current gaps prevent a clear Findings recommendation.
